1. No. "Axis" is the owner's word for a direction of extension, "axis of a figure" and "point" are both barred spatial words, and the phrase names the knot by where it sits. Keep it once, in quotation marks and dated 24 November, pointing to the entry.

2. Ranking: (e) > (h) > (b) > (a) > (c) > (d) > (f) > (g). The entry for (e) must say "at least one of the two members is not its child", because a parent is also an ancestor.
   - **(e) ancestral common knot**: best; it states both descent and meeting.
   - **(h) "common knot by descent"**: same content, but reads as a way of becoming common.
   - **(b)**: "at a remove" names position and does not say removed from what.
   - **(a)**: descent only; it holds whether or not the members ever meet g.
   - **(c)**: "reference" already has three senses, and by lesson 8.7 every common knot is one.
   - **(d)**: the owner's word for a wider family of ideas, and it is a fixing-in-place image.
   - **(f)**: false, because these members never met g, so nothing is regained.
   - **(g)**: "relay" is settled in distributed computing as a forwarder, and g "makes nothing".

3. Name the law; the object needs no word of its own, since "a common knot that is also a common ancestor" says it, with (e) as a defined short form if it recurs. Call the law **ancestor-taking**: a birth may take a distinction that an ancestor holds. I reject "ancestor's share" (reuses the stem of "shared" as "portion"), "inheriting" ("hereditary" is settled in graph theory and topology, and nothing leaves the ancestor) and "re-taking" (the taker never held it before). The sentence "a knot meets only its parents and its children" will then need "under the earlier laws".

4. Use **take**: "the birth takes a shared distinction, which gains a holder". "Re-read" clashes with the owner's "reads" and falsely implies an earlier reading; "pays with" implies giving something up, while the holder count rises. The glossary's "shared: held by two" must become "two or more", or a three-holder distinction has no name; do not call it a "hub".

5. Neither. "Line of descent" means one chain, so using it for the whole set gives it a second meaning, and "the descent of g" reads in plain English as g's ancestry, which points upward. Use **the descendants of g**, and say whether g is included. It is distinct from "part" (it includes dead knots and may span several parts) and from "brood"; "cluster" and "chunk" stay as the owner's quoted words only.
